topic: One Option (Abnormal / Developmental / Health / Human Relationships)
subject: psychology

items.title: The Health Belief Model predicts (some) preventive behaviours
items.claim: Rosenstock's 1974 Health Belief Model proposes that preventive behaviour depends on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers. What's its empirical track record?

options.text: It predicts all health behaviours perfectly

Meta-analyses (Carpenter 2010) find modest predictive power: perceived barriers strongest, perceived benefits moderate, susceptibility and severity weaker. The model under-weights social and emotional factors
It only applies to dental hygiene

items.reveal:
Rosenstock developed the HBM from 1950s public health work on TB screening uptake. It has been applied to vaccination, screening, smoking cessation and COVID behaviours.

Competitors and extensions: Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen 1991, adds intention and perceived control); Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska 1979, stages of change). Behavioural economics (EAST framework: easy, attractive, social, timely) is the more recent UK policy framework.
items.why: Behaviour-change theories provide testable frameworks but rarely explain more than a fraction of variance. Combining them with structural interventions usually outperforms either alone.

items.title: Deinstitutionalisation reduced asylum populations dramatically
items.claim: Following Italy's Basaglia Law (1978), the UK's Care in the Community policy (1980s-90s) and similar reforms elsewhere, what happened to inpatient psychiatric populations?

options.text: Inpatient populations fell by 60-90% in most Western countries by 2000. Outcomes were mixed: better integration for many, but inadequate community resources left some patients homeless or in the criminal justice system
Inpatient care was completely eliminated everywhere

items.reveal:
UK psychiatric inpatient beds: ~150,000 in 1955, ~22,000 by 2010. The shift was driven by both ideology (asylum critique, e.g. Goffman 'Asylums' 1961) and pharmacology (chlorpromazine, 1952).

Where community resources followed (Trieste, Italy under Basaglia), outcomes were generally positive. Where they didn't (UK and US in different ways), gaps in care emerged — over-representation of severely mentally ill people in prisons and homelessness is widely documented.
items.why: Major mental health policy changes have decades-long consequences. The reduction in coercive asylum care was widely accepted; the under-investment in community alternatives is the unresolved part.

items.title: Placebo effects are real but smaller than often claimed
items.claim: Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche's 2010 Cochrane meta-analysis of 234 trials of placebo versus no treatment found:

options.text: Placebos rivalled active drugs for most conditions
Placebos had small effects on continuous subjective outcomes (especially pain and nausea); little effect on objective outcomes; placebo effect in everyday discourse exaggerates the clinical evidence
Placebos had no measurable effect at all

items.reveal:
Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche's Cochrane review pooled randomised trials comparing placebo with no treatment. Effects on objective outcomes (blood pressure, tumour size) were near zero; effects on subjective ones (pain ratings, anxiety) were measurable but modest.

Open-label placebos (Kaptchuk et al. 2010) — patients told they're receiving placebo — still produce effects for some conditions, suggesting expectation and clinical ritual play roles beyond deception.
items.why: Placebos matter for clinical trial design (controls), patient communication and understanding what 'treatment effect' means — but the popular framing oversells what placebos can do.
